evidence_set: Relative risks for 23 outcomes came from 3,992 estimates in 592 prospective and retrospective studies (about 28 million people); exposure from 694 sources; 195 locations, ages 15 to 95 and older. A standard drink is 10 g of ethanol; current drinking is at least one drink in the past 12 months. Uncertainty intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1000 draws carrying sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation. The authors list as limitations that drinking patterns were not modelled, unrecorded consumption may be missed, people under 15 were not assessed and outcomes such as dementia were left out. Funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

GBD 2020 re-reviewed the six alcohol-attributable outcomes that accounted for the most DALYs worldwide with 71 additional studies, dropped lower respiratory infection and used 22 relative-risk curves (five re-fitted, sampled from 0 to 100 g a day; 17 carried over from GBD 2016), relative to non-drinkers. The theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) and the non-drinker equivalence (NDE, the intake at which the weighted risk again equals a non-drinker's) come from a weighted average of the curves, each cause weighted by its share of DALYs (years of life lost plus years lived with disability) in each region, age, sex and year. Across all regions, ages, sexes and years the 2020 TMREL ranged from 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30) standard drinks (10 g) a day; TMREL and NDE varied significantly by age but not by sex or year. Editors' reading of the methods: one curve per cause is applied to every region, so differences between populations come from their mix of diseases.
